questions.q: What is the core governance problem this lesson addresses?
options: Deciding what the governance rules should be in the first place
Each environment enforces the same intended rule through its own native policy language, so maintaining one control means maintaining it three separate times
Azure Policy cannot evaluate any resource created through the Azure portal
AWS Organizations has no mechanism for enforcing account-level guardrails
questions.explain: The rules themselves (no public storage, encryption at rest, mandatory tagging) were already defined; the problem is that Azure Policy, AWS SCPs/Config, and on-prem change control each enforce them in a different native language, which triples the maintenance burden.

questions.q: In the storage example, why did the 'no publicly readable storage' control end up enforced in only two of three environments after six months?
options: The control was never written correctly for any environment
On-prem environments cannot enforce storage controls at all
AWS Config does not support storage-related rules
A new storage SKU shipped on one cloud and that cloud's independently maintained rule was never updated to cover it
questions.explain: Keeping three independently written implementations of one intent in sync forever is unrealistic; a gap opened when one environment's rule wasn't updated for a new resource type.

questions.q: What does a policy-as-code tool like Sentinel or Open Policy Agent actually do in this governance model?
options: It evaluates infrastructure (such as a Terraform plan) against one control expressed once, before it reaches either cloud's native API
It replaces Azure Policy and AWS Config entirely, so neither is needed anymore
It only works for resources already deployed to AWS
It manages on-prem change-control tickets automatically
questions.explain: Sentinel evaluates Terraform plans and OPA evaluates infrastructure configuration using one control written once, catching violations at provisioning time regardless of destination cloud.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why do native policy engines like Azure Policy and AWS Config still matter even with a policy-as-code layer in place?
options: They don't matter anymore once policy-as-code is adopted
They are only useful for cost reporting, not governance
Resources created outside Terraform (portal clicks, emergency changes) still need native, continuous enforcement that policy-as-code at provisioning time can't catch
They are required only for on-prem environments
questions.explain: Policy-as-code catches problems when infrastructure is provisioned through Terraform; native policy engines keep enforcing continuously for anything created outside that path, so both layers are needed.

questions.q: What is the real meaning of 'consistency' across providers, as this lesson frames it?
options: The same question about whether a configuration violates an agreed control produces the same answer regardless of which environment it's in, even though the enforcement syntax differs
Every cloud's policy console must display identical JSON
Azure Policy and AWS SCPs must be rewritten to use identical syntax
On-prem change control must be replaced by a cloud-native policy engine
questions.explain: Consistency is about shared intent and outcome — the same control answered the same way everywhere — not about making the native syntax identical across providers, which generally isn't possible anyway.
